title: Interconnect resilience and gang scheduling diary
body:
Summary:

This is a running diary-style investigation into how transient interconnect degradation (NIC jitter, small packet microbursts, and sporadic link errors) interacts with our gang scheduling semantics and NCCL collective behavior to produce outlier tail latencies and occasionally dropped requests in multi-GPU serving groups. The goal is to capture experimental setups, quick observations, and reproducible commands so follow-ups can be executed by others.

Motivation / context:
- Several customer incidents in Nov 2024 showed intermittent 99.99th percentile latency spikes for small-context chat requests on Dedicated clusters, correlated with small increases in packet drop/retransmit counters on the host NIC.
- Hypothesis: gang scheduling (scheduling all GPUs for a shard at the same start time) makes collectives susceptible to microburst-induced stalls; NCCL sometimes falls back to serialized p2p in these conditions which exacerbates tail latencies.

High-level hypothesis and sub-hypotheses:
1) Microbursts on the host NIC (interrupt pileup / TX queue congestion) cause intermittent small delays in Host staging or RPC completion which push NCCL into slow path or serialize operations.
2) Gang-start behavior increases the instantaneous pressure on interconnect and PCIe host staging so even small transient degradations ripple across replicas.
3) Kernel-level NIC interrupt handling (affinity, coalescing) interacts badly with our IRQ distribution on dense nodes, amplifying jitter for short-lived RPCs.

Testbed (hardware + SW snapshot):
- Node: 8x A100-SXM GPUs, dual 200G HDR NICs (Mellanox), AMD EPYC 7713, 2x PCIe Gen4 switches in host path.
- OS: Ubuntu 22.04, kernel 5.15 + real-time tweaks for isolcpus in experiment runs.
- NCCL: 2.18.3 internal build with debug logging enabled.
- Serving runtime: branch perf/steadybackpressure (git ref: pr/438).
- Workloads: tiny-chat (context 32 tokens, batched request size 1–8), kv-embed (small embedding requests).
- Traffic generator: custom harness (scripts/gang-sched-harness) producing steady baseline QPS and then injecting microbursts (iperf3 traffic + controlled pps spikes via tc/netem).

Methodology / experiment design:
- Repeatable sequence: baseline run (no induced noise) -> NIC microburst injection -> gang-start stagger vs simultaneous -> NIC irq-affinity changes -> host-staging priority adjustments.
- Each experiment run: 30 minutes, record full perf counters: tc counters, ethtool -S, nvidia-smi topo and per-GPU utilization, perf on server process, NCCL_TRACE logs, and kernel dmesg timestamps.
- Metrics: p50/p90/p99/p99.9/p99.99 latencies, number of NCCL fallbacks to p2p or TCP transport, RX/TX queue full events, retry/transmit counters, percentage of requests hitting fallback code path.

Representative commands / knobs used:
- Simulate microburst: tc qdisc add dev eth0 root netem delay 0ms 0.5ms distribution normal limit 1000
- Bursty background: iperf3 -c <peer> -u -b 15G -l 512 -t 60
- IRQ affinity loop: for i in `ls /proc/irq`; do echo 0x$(printf "%x" $cpu_mask) > /proc/irq/$i/smp_affinity; done
- Serving runtime: ./bin/serving --model xxxx --shard-policy gang --start-sync true --trace-nccl=1
- NCCL debug: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO; export NCCL_P2P_LEVEL=NVLINK; export NCCL_TOPO_FILE=/tmp/topo.json

Key runs and quick outcomes (high level):
- Run A (baseline): stable p99.99 ~ 120ms, no NCCL p2p fallbacks, minimal TX queue events.
- Run B (microburst injection at 2x baseline every 10s): periodic p99.99 spikes to 2.5–3s, NCCL logs show fallback to ring->p2p serialization in 12% of collectives during spike windows, ethtool shows tx_restart and drop counters rising.
- Run C (staggered-start: 50ms stagger across 8 GPUs): spike magnitude reduced by ~40% (p99.99 ~ 1.5s), NCCL fallback rate cut to 4%, but throughput slightly reduced.
- Run D (IRQ affinity tuned to spread interrupts across isolated CPUs): tail spikes cut further (p99.99 ~ 1.2s), CPU steal during bursts reduced in perf samples.
- Run E (host staging priority uplift with chrt for staging threads): similar tail reduction but introduced jitter in long-running batches (resource contention observed).

Detailed observations / traces (selected):
- NCCL logs during Spike B (excerpt): "[2024-11-20 16:23:12] NCCL AllReduce: ring fallback triggered: missing progress on comm 0x7f... after 200ms". Multiple repeated timeouts then reconfiguration to pairwise p2p.
- dmesg around same timestamp: repeated "mlx5_core 0000:03:00.0: tx err retry" messages and softirq backlog warnings.
- perf top and stack traces show host staging thread blocked on send() syscall in the kernel for ~180ms windows during bursts.
- ethtool -S counters: tx_dma_busy increased significantly, and netdev_watchdog_timeouts incremented during bursts.

Preliminary root-cause synthesis:
- The immediate trigger is host NIC packet queuing/backpressure during microbursts causing send() to stall briefly. Those stalls translate to late arrival of small control packets used by NCCL during collective handshake. NCCL's software-level timeout triggers fallback or reconfiguration which serializes what would have been parallel collectives, multiplying latency.
- Gang-start amplifies the problem because many GPUs issue collective progress nearly simultaneously, creating a higher synchronization load on the interconnect and the host stacks.
- Kernel IRQ and NIC driver behavior modulate the severity: without good interrupt distribution and TX queue handling, small bursts produce larger stalls.

Mitigations tested (notes):
1) Staggered gang-start (50–200ms): consistently reduces peak tail but at the cost of throughput; tuning required to balance.
2) IRQ affinity tuning: spreading NIC interrupts to multiple isolated cores reduces stall duration significantly on our boxes.
3) Host staging thread priority uplift: helps reduce blocked staging time but can cause CPU contention with other critical threads on busy nodes.
4) NCCL timeouts: increasing timeouts to avoid fallback reduces visible p99.99 spikes but increases risk of long hangs when real link failures occur. Not recommended as primary fix.
5) Lightweight pacing at runtime entry: add micro-delays in serving runtime to smooth the instant pressure. Early runs show synergy with staggered-start.

Risks and tradeoffs:
- Staggering and pacing trade latency distribution for sustained throughput. Customers sensitive to tail latency may accept slightly lower throughput; others may not.
- Driver/OS kernel changes (IRQ handling, TX queue knobs) are node-level and require careful testing across cloud providers and kernel versions.
- Bumping NCCL timeouts hides symptoms but may obscure hard failures.

Action items / next experiments:
- (Short) Automate an experiment matrix that sweeps stagger windows [0,50,100,200,400]ms combined with pacing delays [0,1,2,5]ms and record fallback rate. Owner: Raj Patel. ETA: 2024-11-21.
- (Short) Coordinate with infra to replicate on a different NIC vendor (Chelsio) and alternate kernel (5.19) to validate driver-specific behaviors. Owner: Sofia. ETA: 2024-12-03.
- (Medium) Add a lightweight NCCL transport monitor in runtime that detects early signs of p2p fallbacks and initiates a graceful soft-stagger/fallback policy rather than hard reconfiguration. Design doc stub: github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/issues/489. Owner: Maya. ETA: 2025-01-31.
- (Medium) Evaluate making stagger/pacing configurable per-customer or per-priority class (console controls + rollout). Product discussion required.

Open questions / unresolved puzzles:
- Why do some nodes show no fallout at the same microburst levels? Differences in top-of-rack switch buffering, NIC firmware versions, and PCIe root complex firmware suspected. Need inventory correlation.
- Are there subtle NCCL parameters (SIMPLE_RING_THRESHOLD, COLL_ALGO hints) we can tune to prefer more robust transports under jitter? Requires NCCL upstream tests.
- Can we detect impending microburst conditions proactively at the host level and activate a soft-mode (stagger/pacing) per-serving group?

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Consider a dynamic gang-start window that grows when NIC drop/retry counters trend up and shrinks when stable. Could be combined with per-route QoS tokens.
- Explore kernel-level NIC queue tuning: txqueuelen, gso/sg settings, and skbuff burst coalescing knobs.
- Add better attribution in telemetry: correlate NCCL fallback events with per-packet timestamps (eBPF) to show causality in customer incident retros.

Appendix: raw checklist for reproducibility
- Kernel: ensure controlled kernel boot flags (no scoreboard RT hacks unless running with isolated cpus).
- NIC firmware version: record mlx5_core version and NIC fw via ethtool -i.
- Commands to collect logs (example):
  - sudo nvidia-smi dmon -s u -d 1 > /tmp/gpu-dmon.log &
  - sudo ethtool -S eth0 > /tmp/eth0-snap-$(date +%s).log
  - NCCL logs: export NCCL_DEBUG=INFO; run server with --trace-nccl > /tmp/nccl.log 2>&1
  - Kernel trace: sudo perf record -F 99 -a -g --pid $(pidof serving) sleep 120

If you pick up this thread: please run the automation matrix and push results into the shared sheet linked in the Jira (JIRA-ENG-1724) so we can roll up a heatmap of fallback rate vs stagger/pacing.

-- end diary entry --
